clinicalPearls: Neuropathy caused by variants in NEFL, the gene for the neurofilament light chain, typically inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and classified as an axonal (type 2) CMT.
Electrophysiology can be axonal, demyelinating or intermediate, and the same gene underlies the demyelinating allelic designation CMT1F, so conduction velocities alone do not exclude NEFL.
Presentation ranges from classic distal limb weakness and sensory loss with pes cavus to earlier, more severe childhood-onset forms depending on the variant.
Additional features reported in some patients include hearing loss, tremor and, in severe early-onset cases, more widespread involvement, broadening the phenotype beyond a simple distal neuropathy.
Nerve pathology characteristically shows disorganised neurofilament accumulation and abnormal axonal calibre, reflecting the structural role of the affected protein.
Because velocities may fall into the intermediate range, NEFL should be considered when a family does not fit neatly into demyelinating CMT1 or purely axonal CMT2 categories.
Both dominant and, less commonly, recessive inheritance are described, so inheritance pattern should be interpreted alongside the specific variant.
Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying a pathogenic NEFL variant, with electrophysiology and family history supporting classification.
reference.pathophysiology: CMT2E arises from variants in NEFL, which encodes the neurofilament light chain, one of the intermediate filament proteins that assemble with the medium and heavy neurofilament subunits to form the cytoskeletal network responsible for establishing and maintaining axonal calibre and for supporting axonal transport in large myelinated fibres. Most disease-causing variants act through a dominant-negative or toxic gain-of-function mechanism: mutant light chain disrupts the co-assembly and normal distribution of the neurofilament network, causing aggregation of neurofilaments in neuronal cell bodies and proximal axons, impaired axonal transport, and secondary disturbance of axonal calibre and myelination. This structural failure can manifest electrophysiologically as an axonal, intermediate or even demyelinating neuropathy, which is why NEFL variants underlie both the axonal designation CMT2E and the allelic demyelinating designation CMT1F. The severity spectrum, from adult-onset classic CMT to severe early childhood-onset disease, correlates broadly with how profoundly a given variant destabilises filament assembly, and rarer recessive alleles that reduce functional protein produce their own phenotypes.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2C (TRPV4) with vocal cord and respiratory features
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2D (GARS1) with hand-predominant wasting
Demyelinating CMT1 subtypes, given that NEFL can produce intermediate or demyelinating velocities (CMT1F overlap)
Other axonal CMT2 genes such as MFN2-related CMT2A
Dominant intermediate CMT from other genes
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy when velocities are slowed and progression atypical
Early-onset or congenital hypomyelinating neuropathies in severe childhood presentations
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography, interpreting axonal, intermediate or demyelinating patterns carefully
Targeted NEFL sequencing or a broad hereditary neuropathy gene panel spanning axonal and demyelinating genes
Audiometry where hearing loss is suspected as part of the phenotype
Assessment for tremor and its impact on function
Nerve biopsy in selected atypical cases, which may show neurofilament accumulation and altered axonal calibre
Detailed pedigree analysis to clarify dominant versus recessive inheritance and variant segregation
Foot and gait assessment to document pes cavus and distal weakness for baseline and follow-up
redFlags: Severe early childhood-onset weakness or delayed motor milestones indicating an aggressive variant
Rapid clinical progression or steroid-responsiveness suggesting a superimposed inflammatory neuropathy
New or worsening hearing loss requiring audiological input
Marked functional deterioration in gait or hand use affecting safety
Atypical widespread neurological signs prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Outlook depends strongly on the specific variant and age at onset: adult-onset disease often follows a slowly progressive course with retained ambulation, whereas severe childhood-onset forms can cause substantial early disability. Progression and additional features such as hearing loss vary between families.
pitfalls: Excluding NEFL because nerve conduction velocities are slowed, overlooking the demyelinating CMT1F overlap
Misclassifying an intermediate-velocity neuropathy and testing only axonal or only demyelinating gene sets
Attributing an inflammatory-looking, slowly slowed picture to CIDP and treating immunologically without genetic testing
Assuming inheritance is always dominant and missing rarer recessive presentations
Failing to screen for associated features such as hearing loss and tremor that support the diagnosis
references: Clinical review of neurofilament-related hereditary neuropathies
